covers.quote: The word ‘disinterested’ means ‘impartial’ and ‘unbiased by personal interest’.

parts.quote: The judge’s deliberation was disinterested and considered.
The invitation to the concert was wasted on me because I’m uninterested in jazz music.

rules.quote: ‘Disinterested’ is often used to mean ‘uninterested’, but this use is not correct.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Disinterested’ is used to mean not interested, indifferent or unconcerned, rather than impartial or unbiased.
when: Distinguish lack of interest from impartiality; ‘disinterested’ is correct for impartiality.
rules.why: G-4: the explicit rejection of a usage states the rule; the definitions clarify its scope rather than creating additional rules.

covers.quote: The word ‘dove’ is the past tense of ‘dive’ in American English.

parts.quote: Bystanders dived into the creek to help the drowning swimmer.

rules.quote: In Australian English, write ‘dived’ to use the past tense of the verb ‘to dive’.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Dove’ is used as the past tense of ‘dive’ in Australian English.
when: Applies to the past-tense verb, not the noun ‘dove’.
The instruction concerns Australian English; the page identifies verbal ‘dove’ as American English.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: one past-tense spelling check, limited to Australian English and stated in the body instruction.

parts.quote: The paperwork may take a few weeks to come through but, for all intents and purposes, you are hired.

rules.quote: The correct expression is ‘for all intents and purposes’, meaning ‘in every practical sense’.
rules.violation_condition: The expression is written as ‘for all intensive purposes’ instead of ‘for all intents and purposes’.
rules.why: G-4: the body explicitly identifies the correct expression; the heading merely names the competing forms.

covers.quote: The exception is a court decision; write this as ‘judgment’.

parts.quote: You can speak to one of our counsellors without fearing judgement.
Please cite the High Court’s most recent judgment in the issues paper.

rules.violation_condition: ‘Judgment’ is used outside the court-decision sense, or ‘judgement’ is used for a court decision.
when: Use ‘judgment’ for a court decision.
Use ‘judgement’ otherwise.
rules.why: G-2: the court-decision exception changes which spelling is required within one spelling-choice check.

covers.quote: When referring to a specific qualification, use ‘Master of [area of study]’.

parts.quote: He completed his master degree last year.
Having a Master of Arts helped her gain the promotion.
The university offered several master degrees to postgraduate students.

rules.violation_condition: A generic master-level degree is written as ‘masters degree’ or ‘master’s degree’, or a specific qualification is not styled ‘Master of [area of study]’.
when: Use ‘master degree’ for a generic reference, and ‘master degrees’ for the plural.
Use ‘Master of [area of study]’ when referring to a specific qualification.
rules.why: G-2: generic references and specific qualifications are conditional forms within one degree-naming check.

covers.quote: Use ‘program’ for the titles of new programs based on government policy.
Use ‘programme’ only when it is part of the formal name of an existing program.

parts.quote: One of the most challenging aspects of our work is designing programs that can be implemented quickly.
The Prescription Shopping Programme lets medical practitioners check their patients’ prescription histories.

rules.quote: Use ‘program’ rather than ‘programme’, including for computer programs.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Programme’ is used other than as part of the formal name of an existing program.
when: Applies to computer programs and titles of new programs based on government policy.
‘Programme’ is allowed when it is part of the formal name of an existing program.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: new titles and the existing-formal-name exception belong to the same spelling check.

covers.quote: It is not accepted as standard Australian English.

parts.quote: Our aim is for all staff to have access to this training, regardless of location.
The following instructions will work regardless of which mobile platform you use.
These are interesting times but we must carry on regardless.

rules.why: G-4: the instruction and the rejection of ‘irregardless’ express one word-choice rule.

parts.quote: If I had known we were over budget, I would have changed the scope of the contract.
This would’ve spared us a lot of stress
At the very least, we would of avoided the overspend.

rules.quote: Always write ‘would have’ or the contracted form ‘would’ve’.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Would of’ is used in place of ‘would have’ or ‘would’ve’.
when: Both ‘would have’ and ‘would’ve’ are acceptable.
rules.why: G-3 and G-4: the full and contracted forms are alternatives within one check; the explicit rejection restates that check.
